title: Is Anthropic on the cusp of RSI? Inside the redacted METR report
content:

### AI is now building AI twice as fast [[00:00:00]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=0)

**Luisa Rodriguez:** I just got through reading what may be [the scariest AI report](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) I’ve ever seen. [METR](https://metr.org/), an independent group that assesses AI risk, spent 11 weeks going through Anthropic’s internal data. They found Anthropic is now improving its AI about twice as fast as it was a year ago. And the main reason seems to be that its AI is helping build the next version of itself.

The reason that’s scary is, if Anthropic is able to hand off a big share of coding and experiments to its AI, the next, more powerful model arrives sooner. That version then does even more of the work, so the one after that arrives sooner still. And each iteration leaves [less time to verify](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ajeya-cotra-transformative-ai-crunch-time/) that the new model is safe before it’s helping build the next one.

AI experts have been [warning about this for years](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/tom-davidson-how-quickly-ai-could-transform-the-world/), and there’s a term for it. It’s called [recursive self-improvement](https://80000hours.org/articles/how-ai-driven-feedback-loops-could-make-things-very-crazy-very-fast/), and if METR’s right, Anthropic might be on the cusp of it right now. Some of those experts thought this was further off. This report changed their minds.

### 11 weeks inside Anthropic [[00:01:09]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=69)

Anthropic has [drawn itself a line](https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy): the point where its AI speeds up its research enough to make two years of progress in one. By the time it reaches that point, it plans to have taken serious, specific steps to make its AI [harder to steal](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/sella-nevo-securing-ai-model-weights/), and to monitor everything happening inside its own AI development.

In its [August risk report](https://assets.claude.com/f61d49fa5596956a5dec75fea0e973bf6a6a8378.pdf), Anthropic said it didn’t believe its models had reached that line. They invited METR to [look into that claim](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-rd-section-anthropic-risk-report-august-2026-review/), and gave them 11 weeks inside the company.

They were given access to data almost no one outside Anthropic has seen: internal test scores, data on how its AI is trained, and interviews with the people building the models. They didn’t have unrestricted access, but METR says [Anthropic shared a lot more](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) than they expected.

### Two years of progress in one year [[00:01:59]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=119)

At the end of its investigation, METR found that, as of October, Anthropic was improving its AI [about twice as fast](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) as it was a year ago, at least on the kinds of [tasks that we can easily measure](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/beth-barnes-ai-safety-evals/). That’s METR’s best guess, though they say the true speed-up could be anywhere between 1.3 and 3 times as fast.

One of their main pieces of evidence was Anthropic’s test scores for every model it’s built, including three internal models that are better than any the public has seen. If you plot those over time, around October of last year, the line suddenly gets about twice as steep.

Personally, I find “twice as fast” hard to wrap my head around, so let me try to make it feel real. In late 2023, Claude was a chatbot. It couldn’t [look at a photo](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-family). It couldn’t even [look things up on the internet](https://claude.com/resources/articles/web-search).

By late 2025, Anthropic said it could work on its own for [more than 30 hours](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-sonnet-4-5), building an entire [Slack-style app](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/787524/anthropic-releases-claude-sonnet-4-5-in-latest-bid-for-ai-agents-and-coding-supremacy) with no human stepping in. That was two years of progress.

Then, just a year later, AI helped [settle a math problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture) that had defeated generations of mathematicians for 87 years. That’s what METR means by making two years’ worth of progress in one.

### Is AI causing the speed-up? [[00:03:19]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=199)

METR’s next question was: what’s behind that speed-up? They [ruled out the simplest explanation](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/): more computing power. Anthropic is definitely using more, but that isn’t where the speed-up is coming from.

Other obvious explanations, like a hiring spree, a trove of new data, or a big research breakthrough, may have kicked it off, but they can’t explain why it’s lasted this long.

Taking everything into account, METR’s best guess is that about 80% of today’s speed-up comes from Anthropic [using its own AI](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/2026-agi-timelines/) to help do its research. But Anthropic redacted most of the reasoning behind that number in the public report, including the majority of the evidence that METR found most convincing. METR admits this means we have to rely on their judgement much more than would be ideal.

But they were able to share some of the evidence. First, a bunch of [Anthropic’s own researchers](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/#interview-quotes) say AI has sped up their area a lot. One said, “I’ve seen us discovering very promising directions entirely because people can spam 10 ideas at Claude and just see what sticks.”

On their own, impressions like these wouldn’t be that convincing.

But they line up with the timing. The speed-up seems to start in October 2025, right around when Claude got good enough to write code [on its own for hours](https://metr.org/time-horizons/) at a time.

Here’s the second piece of evidence. Claude isn’t doing major research on its own yet, but researchers say they’re seeing early signs of it in several parts of the training process.

[Anthropic has its own numbers](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development) on this. Earlier this year, Claude was doing almost none of its research work end to end. By August, it was doing about a quarter, though still with humans supervising.

So METR’s read is that AI’s role in its own development has been growing, and that it’s now the main reason Anthropic is speeding up.

### No signs of slowing down [[00:05:15]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=315)

There’s nothing obvious that’s going to slow it down. AI building AI is different from other technologies. The better your AI gets, the faster it helps you build the next one.

That loop only stops if it hits a bottleneck, like running short on computing power, training data, or ideas for algorithmic improvements. [METR looked for all three](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) and didn’t find anything likely to get in the way in the next year.

They aren’t confident. Their picture changed several times as they got more information. But METR says they [can’t rule out things getting](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-rd-section-anthropic-risk-report-august-2026-review/) a lot faster in the next six months. They even say the speed-up itself could be increasing.

If the speed-up does keep climbing, then two years of progress in one year could become two years of progress in six months, then three months, then six weeks.

Two years ago, AI couldn’t [count the Rs](https://techcrunch.com/2024/08/27/why-ai-cant-spell-strawberry/) in ‘strawberry.’ This year, [Anthropic’s Mythos](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/claude-mythos-hacking-alignment/) found [thousands of serious security flaws](https://www.anthropic.com/glasswing) that nobody knew about in every major operating system and every major web browser.

After a few more rounds of speed-up, I honestly can’t imagine what AI is going to be able to do.

This is all uncomfortably close to the way things play out in [AI 2027](https://ai-2027.com/), a well-known prediction scenario written two years ago based on AI progress and the geopolitical situation at the time. In [its darker ending](https://ai-2027.com/race), by the end of 2027, AI is superintelligent and humans have lost any real chance of controlling their future. By 2030, it’s [killed almost everyone on Earth](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-extinction-explained/) with biological weapons.

In that forecast, the speed-up in AI research METR just found doesn’t happen until early 2027. If METR’s right about this, we may already be a [few months ahead of schedule](https://x.com/RyanGreenblatt/status/2118447235289817503).

### Could METR be wrong? [[00:07:21]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=441)

All of this rests on METR being right. So how solid is their finding that Anthropic is now making progress twice as fast?

METR [redid the analysis lots of ways](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/): with different statistical methods, changing which benchmarks they used, leaving out certain models. Almost every version still showed progress happening around twice as fast.

The strongest pushback I’ve seen comes from the philosopher [Toby Ord](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/toby-ord-recursive-self-improvement-agi-timelines/). He points out that that line of test scores could be read another way. Mythos came from a much bigger training run, and those usually bring a one-off jump in ability. Allow for that, and the line only shows progress [about 1.4 times as fast](https://x.com/tobyordoxford/status/2118677731248673046).

That’s a fair point about the test scores. But as AI safety researcher [Buck Shlegeris points out](https://x.com/bshlgrs/status/2119255143439048733), they’re not the main reason METR reached their conclusion. They’re just the only part of their analysis that wasn’t redacted. And METR says the redacted evidence made them take the twice-as-fast finding more seriously.

Another reason some people are sceptical: compared with other companies’ models, rather than its own past, Anthropic’s speed-up looks smaller. METR says that could mean Anthropic was just catching up, or that its models were less tuned to the tests than its rivals’.

But you can partly check that with public data. An economist, [Karthik Tadepalli](https://blog.karthiktadepalli.com/p/metr-anthropic-report), tried, expecting to cast doubt on METR’s result. Instead, he says he came away convinced.

But the biggest caveat is that all of this is measured on tasks that are easy to grade, like a coding problem with the right answer. We don’t know if messier, real-world work has sped up as much. But that cuts both ways. METR points out that AI’s math scores haven’t sped up much, even as [Millennium Prize Problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium_Prize_Problems) that have stumped mathematicians for decades are now being solved.

A lot of people I trust have changed their minds because of this report. [Ryan Greenblatt](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ryan-greenblatt-ai-automation-sabotage-takeover/), who studies these risks for a living, says he was [seriously wrong](https://x.com/RyanGreenblatt/status/2118447235289817503). He’d expected much less speed-up this year, and now calls the report a big update towards superintelligence within one to two years.

[Buck Shlegeris](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/buck-shlegeris-ai-control-scheming/) now thinks there’s [about a one in three chance](https://x.com/bshlgrs/status/2120271165692461316) AI companies build superintelligence within the next year. And if that happens, he thinks [AIs will probably take over](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/loss-of-control/).

Nobody knows exactly how much AI is speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress. But whether progress is 1.4 times as fast or two and a half times as fast, AI is now helping build better AI. And nothing METR found suggests that’s about to stop.

### Has Anthropic crossed its own line? [[00:10:18]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=618)

I want to come back to Anthropic’s line: two years of progress in one. If METR’s right, isn’t Anthropic already there?

Apparently Anthropic didn’t think so, at least as of August. [Their last public report](https://assets.claude.com/f61d49fa5596956a5dec75fea0e973bf6a6a8378.pdf) said progress had sped up “by less than a factor of 2.” But when METR [ran Anthropic’s private numbers](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-rd-section-anthropic-risk-report-august-2026-review/), they came out at 1.97.

Just as I was finishing this video, Anthropic answered this question itself. Its [latest IPO filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026072484/anthropicpbc-sx1ax2.htm) says it has now crossed its own line, based on what it expects from its next models and based on how fast things are moving now. It hasn’t said what it’s going to do about this, only that it’s evaluating the implications.

Anthropic is either at that line or very close to it. And I want to see Anthropic do [what it said it would do](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/0bacdc8440ea96e62a8766d99ebe1d4eea6d5f3a.pdf). That means security strong enough to stop the world’s [best-resourced hackers](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/infosecurity-compilation/), including governments, and tracking everything that happens in its AI development, so it would catch an employee or [an AI doing something it shouldn’t](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugging-face-hack/).

But to be honest, even if Anthropic does all of that, it isn’t nearly enough.

### What needs to change [[00:11:33]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=693)

Recursive self-improvement — AI building better AI — may be close. The AI companies aren’t stopping because they think that if they do, their competitors will just keep going. And those competitors might be even less careful. So if the companies won’t stop themselves, [the government needs to step in](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how/).

[Alex Bores](https://x.com/AlexBores/status/2118494668769878037), a New York state legislator, is calling on Congress to ban AI companies from fully automating their own research. And some version of that proposal has supporters from [Bernie Sanders](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/bernie-sanders-greg-casar-propose-ai-superintelligence-ban-20-year-jai-rcna599460) to [Steve Bannon](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/prince-harry-steve-bannon-unlikely-allies-ai-superintelligence-ban/). I think that’s exactly the right place to start.

Anthropic deserves credit for agreeing to this kind of outside investigation. OpenAI, Google, and the rest could be speeding up just as fast, and we wouldn’t know.

But Anthropic set the terms here. They decided what information METR could see, what made it into the final public report, and whether METR will be invited back. They also [tightened their redaction rules](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) in the final week, forcing METR to rework their public report and push back publication.

And METR says that, while writing their report, they were worried that being too critical could make companies less willing to let them in next time. That’s the problem with [outside scrutiny](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hold-frontier-ai-companies-accountable/) that only happens when the company agrees to it.

So at an absolute minimum, every frontier company should have to report how much AI is speeding up its own research, and have [someone independent](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/beth-barnes-ai-safety-evals/) check what they say.

### What you can do [[00:13:12]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi/?t=792)

If you remember early 2020, you know how this kind of thing feels. In February, COVID seemed like a far-off problem, or even fearmongering. By April, [half the world was in lockdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_April_2020).

That’s what happens when something keeps speeding up. It looks manageable right up until it isn’t. And COVID spread at a fairly steady rate. With AI, the worry is that the rate itself will keep increasing.

This might just be the beginning of an almost incomprehensible speed-up in the [progress of literally everything](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/will-macaskill-century-in-a-decade-navigating-intelligence-explosion/), for better and for worse.

If you’re wondering what you can do: if you’ve been considering [pivoting to work on this issue](https://80000hours.org/ai/), now is the time to do it. That might mean [working directly on these problems](https://jobs.80000hours.org/?refinementList%5Btags_area%5D%5B0%5D=AI+safety+%26+policy&jb_source=podcast__episodes__metr-anthropic-recursive-self-improvement-rsi). It might mean finding a more flexible job so you can take on projects on the side. Or it might mean donating more, and [thinking hard about where](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/luke-muehlhauser-ai-safety-grantmaking-founding/).

And talk about it. Share this video, or your own worries, with the people in your life. Most people still have no idea this is happening.

Or learn more about recursive self-improvement and [why it’s so dangerous](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i30jVPqQeOM&t=204). We’ll leave some links below. If you’re not sure where to start, we have a [free AI career advising tool](https://app.80000hours.org/) that can talk you through it. It can suggest options and support you along the way.

Because if things change as fast as this report suggests, there may not be long before what we do stops making much of a difference. And when that happens, I want to be able to say we gave it everything we had.

title: Help Us Respond to Enormous Global Needs: Why We’re Recommending the All Grants Fund
content:
Each year we reflect on the opportunities our research has identified and how we think donors can have the greatest impact. For the past three years, we’ve encouraged donors to choose among our three [Giving Funds](https://www.givewell.org/our-giving-funds) based on their preferences: the Top Charities Fund for those who wanted the most certainty, the All Grants Fund for those who wanted to support the highest-impact opportunities we have identified, and the Unrestricted Fund for those those who wanted to support GiveWell’s operations as well as the full spectrum of our grantmaking.

**This year, we recommend that donors give to the [All Grants Fund](https://www.givewell.org/all-grants-fund).**

GiveWell is growing quickly. We expect our grantmaking in 2026 to exceed $1 billion, more than double what we committed in 2025, and we expect to grow further in the years ahead. From 2027 through 2032, we’re aiming to grant at least [$2.5 billion in new malaria funding](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking/), and potentially much more. In addition, in 2027 alone, we expect to grant more than $1 billion to program areas outside malaria, and we think we could grant more with additional funding. At this scale, flexibility matters more than it used to.

Supporting the All Grants Fund provides us with this flexibility. Donations to the All Grants Fund can be used to support the full range of GiveWell’s grantmaking. We make grants from the All Grants Fund to those opportunities that we believe will have the greatest impact—that may mean, for example, supporting a Top Charity program, piloting new programs, or funding research that we think will help us direct more funding to highly cost-effective programs in the future.

The Top Charities Fund, in contrast, can only be granted to [four programs](https://www.givewell.org/charities/top-charities). We continue to think highly of those programs and believe they can use more funding.[1](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/11/12/help-us-respond-to-enormous-global-needs-why-were-recommending-the-all-grants-fund/)As donations grow, giving to the Top Charities Fund may outpace what the Top Charity programs can absorb at our current cost-effectiveness threshold. If that happens, donations to the fund would wait until new opportunities at those programs open up. We recently removed the time requirement for committing funds from the Top Charities Fund to ensure that all donations to the fund would be used for programs meeting our cost-effectiveness threshold. For example, our largest grant to date went to one of our Top Charity programs: in August we made a [$276 million grant to the Against Malaria Foundation (AMF)](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/08/24/announcing-our-largest-grant-to-date/) for insecticide-treated nets in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

[![Image 1: Graphic with 16 boxes containing text, four of which are enclosed in another box. ](https://blog.givewell.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Top-Charities-Fund-lower-right@1x.png)](https://blog.givewell.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Top-Charities-Fund-lower-right@1x.png)

This year so far, we’ve made 40 grants using donations to the All Grants Fund. These grants have supported Top Charity programs such as AMF’s nets and Helen Keller’s vitamin A supplementation, along with HIV prevention and services, vaccination outreach, scoping for water disinfection programs, coverage surveys, and research on new tools to prevent malaria, among many others.[2](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/11/12/help-us-respond-to-enormous-global-needs-why-were-recommending-the-all-grants-fund/)You can see the full range of grants supported by the All Grants Fund in the [GiveWell grants database](https://airtable.com/appaVhon0jdLt1rVs/shrvW7wFycJSylxeP).

While we are often less certain about the individual grants we make via our All Grants Fund, since they include more experimental opportunities and programs that have a less robust evidence base, we think that—in aggregate—these grants represent the highest-impact use of donations. We want to put every dollar to use where we expect it will do the most good, and the All Grants Fund enables us to do that.

If you’d like to support our ability to continue doing what we do, we also welcome donations to our [Unrestricted Fund](https://www.givewell.org/unrestricted-fund), which can be used for any GiveWell priority, including our operating expenses. If we raise more unrestricted funding than we need for our operating costs, we will [grant the excess](https://blog.givewell.org/2024/07/18/what-if-we-have-extra/) to highly cost-effective programs that our research has identified. This is a great fit for donors who are excited about GiveWell’s work and trust us to prioritize between our operations and grantmaking.

Thank you for your trust in our research and your partnership in helping people as much as we can.

title: Ten minutes a day
content:
You can’t become fluent in a foreign language in ten minutes a day, even if you try for months.

On the other hand, here are a dozen things many of us can do (or do better) if we stick with it:

Three-ball juggling  
Touch typing  
Rubik’s Cube  
Drawing  
Mental math  
Memorizing a deck of cards or people’s names  
Meditating  
History or geography  
Finding joy in small things  
Typography  
Ukulele  
Italic handwriting  
Morse code  
Excel and HTML

There are two hard parts:

1.   The seven minutes after minute three
2.   Doing it again tomorrow

“I can’t do that,” might often be more honestly reported as, “I haven’t chosen to be able to do that.”

title: Watch Norway’s Lice-Zapping Robots Protect Salmon Farms
content:
Humans and bears aren’t the only animals that find salmon delicious. Salmon lice, small marine crustaceans, attach themselves to the fish and make a meal of their blood, mucus, and skin cells (not my favorite part of the salmon, but it takes all types). These parasites are also the scourge of Norwegian salmon farmers, who keep their shoals in net pens in the Atlantic Ocean.

Removing them is required by law, but it’s a real pain. They’ve become resistant to pharmaceutical deterrents and traditional delousing methods involve hot water baths, scrubbing, and general rough handling, which can damage or kill the fish. While some farms have employed cleaner wrasses to feed on the bloodsuckers, they’ve proved difficult to keep alive.

**Read more: “**[**Cocaine Fish: How Salmon Behave When Amped Up on Coke**](https://nautil.us/cocaine-fish-how-salmon-behave-when-amped-up-on-coke-1279995)**”**

So what can be done?

Obviously the only solution is zapping the parasites with a high-powered laser guided by artificial intelligence. At least that’s what the company Stingray Marine Solutions AS came up with. According to the company, their optical delousing system is already watching over 20 to 25 percent of farmed Norwegian salmon.

The system consists of robotic “submarines” that float in the net pens. The robots bathe the salmon in blue light to enhance the contrast of the lice against the salmon skin which allows the artificial intelligence to detect the parasites. Once the target is acquired, a high-powered laser capable of firing five pulses per second superheats the louse, killing it.

It looks incredibly cool in action:

But does it work?

Per a [study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0044848625007963) the company paid for, it does. A team of their own researchers combined public data on weekly lice counts and treatments from 845 Norwegian sites with the manufacturer’s records of which sites and weeks used optical delousing. They found sites with the laser system in place required fewer additional delousing treatments compared to sites without them. “Our results show that sites relying on optical delousing exhibit a 50 percent lower weekly treatment probability,” the researchers wrote.

However, a [survey](https://www.vetinst.no/rapporter-og-publikasjoner/rapporter/2025/norwegian-fish-health-report-2024) of salmon farmers conducted by the Norwegian Veterinary Institute found mixed results. According to their results, 75 percent of salmon farmers had experience with lasers, and 17 percent of those said they helped them avoid at least one or two delousing treatments. But 56 percent of laser-using farmers said they weren’t sure if they were having any effect. In open-ended questions, the farmers reported the systems were better at delousing when lice populations were low. Additionally, some said the software may be undercounting the parasites (compared to manual counting), which makes their effectiveness difficult to determine.

So lasers may not be the ultimate solution to Norway’s salmon lice problem (yet). But they do look cool doing their jobs. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Trail Cameras Show Coyotes Using the World’s Largest Wildlife Crossing
content:
The new Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, a bridge that connects two portions of Callifornia’s Santa Monica Mountains separated by 10 lanes of highway, has its first beneficiaries: A coyote used it to cross the 101 freeway on October 28th, and a few days later, a second coyote did the same.

The crossing, which measures around 210 feet in length and 174 feet in width, isn’t finished yet, with the official opening scheduled for December, but it’s encouraging that it’s already helping animals get from point A to point B without having to risk their lives getting through L.A. traffic. The $114 million project will also include a second wildlife bridge and 13 acres of restored habitat. It connects the Simi Hills in the north to the Santa Monica Mountains in the south.

The crossing under construction. _Credit: Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing_

Wildlife expected to benefit from the crossing include bobcats, badgers, black bears, deer, birds of prey, foxes, and mountain lions. Since 2002, at least a dozen mountain lions have been killed on the 101. Moreover, GPS trackers [have shown](https://laist.com/news/climate-environment/heres-how-la-is-going-to-construct-the-worlds-largest-wildlife-crossing) other lions approach the road, but then turn back—which has led to physical abnormalities in the isolated populations.

“This is more than just about whether animals use the crossing,” Seth Riley, of the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area, said in a [statement](https://www.nps.gov/samo/learn/news/national-park-service-to-begin-scientific-monitoring-at-wallis-annenberg-wildlife-crossing.htm). “We want to understand how effective it is in reconnecting an ecosystem that’s been divided by the freeway for decades. That’s a much bigger scientific question and answering it will take years.”

A coyote finds its way over the bridge. _Credit: NPS/Jeff Sikich_

The new structure owes a significant debt to P-22, [the Mountain Lion of Hollywood](https://mountainlion.org/2023/12/15/p22-legacy/) that made it across two freeways before eventually being euthanized in 2022 due to health complications. The story of P-22—and the iconic photos of him—helped raise awareness of conservation efforts in L.A., and the need for crossings that would expand the habitat available to these animals.

Even before the official opening, we already know it’s working. As one [Facebook post](https://www.facebook.com/p22mountainlionofhollywood/posts/were-not-officially-open-yet-but-that-didnt-stop-our-first-wildlife-visitor-from/1666841308145782/) put it: “To everyone who wondered how wildlife would know where to go without signs... apparently, they’ve figured it out.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: You May be Able to Get 43 More Minutes of Work Done if You Change Your Desk
content:
Have you ever wished you had an extra hour in the day? Well, if you’ll settle for roughly 45 minutes, I’ve got good news for you. A new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.3390/tae2030021) in _Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics_ found that workers can squeeze 43 minutes of extra productivity out of their day, just by using a sit-stand desk.

A team of occupational and public health researchers from Texas A&M University discovered the productivity benefits of these adjustable-height desks, which exploded in popularity around the time sitting was declared “[the new smoking](https://www.cnbc.com/2014/08/18/why-your-chair-might-be-killing-you.html),” after studying more than 10,000 workers who worked at a large California energy company. They surveyed the workers about their comfort and tracked their computer activity digitally, capturing everything from keystrokes and mouse clicks to words typed and typos.

**Read more: “**[**Your Boss Is Watching You**](https://nautil.us/your-boss-is-watching-you-1284806)**”**

They found that workers who used the height-adjustable desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time per day, compared with just 2.95 hours among those using old-fashioned sit-only desks. Over a year, that adds up to roughly 170 hours of work or four 40-hour workweeks. The sit-standers also made more keystrokes and typed more words (although this speedy typing resulted in slightly more typos). Both groups were equally comfortable (or uncomfortable).

The productivity gains could add up to big bucks, too. According to their back-of-the-envelope calculations using a $52 per hour wage, sit-stand desks may be able to generate roughly $9,000 in annual productivity value per employee (this is where your boss’s eyes turn into dollar signs).

“Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” study author Mark Benden said in a [statement](https://stories.tamu.edu/news/2026/11/11/want-to-be-more-productive-at-work-show-your-boss-this-study/). “The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way.”

There’s one caveat, however: This wasn’t a randomized controlled trial. Instead of being randomly assigned workstations, employees were allowed to choose whether they wanted a sitting or standing desk as part of a company wellness program. It’s possible that the more conscientious workers simply opted for adjustable desks.

Still, there are countless studies on the health risks posed by living a sedentary life, so if you don’t want a height-adjustable desk for your productivity, consider one for your health. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Shapes and Colors of a Near-Death Experience
content:
Near-death experiences are more common than many of us might think: Some studies [estimate](https://peerj.com/articles/7585.pdf) that between four and eight percent of the global population has had one, as have [up to](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12529-011-9209-y) 23 percent of [cardiac arrest survivors](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1015258818660). These journeys into the borderlands of consciousness tend to feature a few common perceptual themes: ghostly figures and bright lights, tunnels, a sense of peace and calm. But questions about the nature of such experiences and how such perceptual phenomena arise abound.

Recently, visual artist and neurophenomenology researcher France Lerner and her colleagues asked 50 individuals who reported near-death experiences (NDE) to divide their recollections of them into phases, to reconstruct them using drawings of geometric shapes, and to describe the colors they perceived. The participants reported entering four types of spaces: cones, broad arches, gentle curves, and spaces resembling the inside of an egg. The cone shapes, the researchers note, look a lot like the tunnels ending in bright lights so characteristic of NDE stories.

**Read More: “**[**The New Science of the Near-Death Experience**](https://nautil.us/the-new-science-of-the-near-death-experience-1279957)**”**

The study participants reported that the tunnels were generally colorless, while some of the arched spaces were vividly hued. The authors suggest that the cone shapes resemble what happens when peripheral vision narrows, as in fainting from low blood pressure, certain eye conditions, or when the eyes and the brain are deprived of oxygen. In those conditions, color sensitivity fades to the edges of vision. In addition, one of the brain’s visual pathways handles motion and brightness but is less good at managing color, which might explain the sensation of rushing through a tunnel towards a bright light. Lerner and her colleagues published their [results](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1760389/full) in _Frontiers in Psychology_.

They point out that these results come with numerous caveats: The NDEs happened a median of about 15 years earlier, and some of them almost 80 years earlier. Participants chose from a menu of shapes, which could have influenced what they drew, and the researcher wasn’t blind to the hypothesis. No second person classified the drawings and there was no comparison group. But the authors say it’s an exploratory framework, not proof of universal motifs.

Lerner has been studying the spatial geometry, and visual patterns of movement and color characteristic to near-death experiences since she started her PhD in art and science in 2012 at the neurological department at the Liège University Hospital in Belgium. We spoke about why near-death experiences are difficult to study, how her work as an artist informs her research, and how the features of a near-death experience resemble a Rorschach test.

**Why are near death experiences so difficult to study?**

Because they are retrospective, first of all. It is very difficult to study them while they’re happening, so you have to find ways to measure what people tell you after the fact. The categorization of near-death experiences is also not very precise, and we can see now that they overlap with other types of experiences like psychedelic experiences, like meditation, that are non-life threatening.

Collecting individual descriptions of the phenomenology of the near-death experience is a good way of escaping this division between skeptic and mystic when it comes to these experiences. People have a religious, dogmatic, even theological view of near-death experiences. I’m trying to really bring it back to science in terms of neural correlates, what’s happening in the visual system.

**With this study, you asked your participants to divide their near-death experience into phases, and then reconstruct the experiences using geometric drawings. What were you trying to find out?**

Because these experiences are so emotional, people who have them overestimate or underestimate temporality. That’s why I asked the participants in my study to segment the experience into pieces, to get around this distortion of temporality.

Ordering an experience into chronological pieces helps you understand how it is organized in space. These spaces act like a container. Each scene has a special component. And then you start to make sense of the chronology and also to make a clear distinction between near-death experiences or NDEs and out of body experiences or OBEs.

In the OBE, it’s a little bit like being in virtual reality, where your body is physically in one place, but when you have the headset on, you are feeling like you are somewhere else. You become just a point of view.

The geometry is actually the visual field. These spaces that you see and, and this phenomena we’re writing about now is visual metamorphosia. Visual metamorphosia is when your visual field is inverted or oriented in different ways. This can happen to fighter pilots when they lack oxygen.

**Are you going to continue to investigate near death experiences?**

We started to develop a software program in 3D that will be for users and researchers to collect data across near-death experiences, out of body experiences, and also meditative and drug-induced states. I want to make the study of these experiences more rigorous, which means to have it digitalized. We also want to establish parallels with this new field called computational phenomenology, which bridges first person human experience with the structures of digital code and AI.

**You’re an artist, and I was looking at your**[**website**](https://www.francelerner.com/lernerfrance)**and some of your installations. I noticed that one of the series is titled “resuscitation.” Is there any connection between that work and your work on near death experiences?**

When you are an artist, you have this experience of creation, and creation is this moment where there is no time. It’s a kind of transcendental experience. So it’s very similar in some sense to the near-death experience, to any experience where time is distorted in some way: meditation, psychedelics. The installation you’re referring to is quite old, but there is always this connection between life and death.

This piece was actually quite personal, but I don’t mind because it was a victory. My daughter was sick. She had cancer when she was a baby. And we made it through. She’s 23. She’s alive and kicking. But this installation was about motherhood and the fact that it’s not as pretty and ideal as our stories of it often are.

It’s also survival. The mother cat will hold onto her baby by the scruff of the neck. It was about this. But also, my dad was a professor of medicine, and so it was always clear to me that there’s lots of life in [?]death and a lot of death in life. It’s a continuum, not a sharp border. But I’m a pure physicalist. I think that when you are brain dead, there is nothing left.

**You mentioned in the study a number of Western and non-Western artists who have depicted altered states, including near death experiences. I wondered, do any of those works especially speak to you or could they inform scientific research?**

I think it’s very interesting to look at the fact that we all have almost the same eyes, but the interpretation varies. It’s like with the Rorschach test. You will project your own culture onto whatever is in front of you. You will see whatever you need to see at the time when you are going to pass from one state to the other state.

The Tibetan book of Dead describes it very precisely. If you need to see angels there to help you, you will see angels. Our brain is great at producing hallucinations to help us. But the physiology of the visual system plays a part. It gives us clay to work with. Then some people interpret what they see as a river. For others it’s a tunnel. It’s amazing how we are prone to such interpretations. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Was Einstein Seduced by a Russian Honeypot Operation?
content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down today just days after he [admitted](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/technology/nvidia-investigation-jensen-huang-china.html) to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The relationship raised alarms at United States intelligence agencies, who reportedly believed his paramour, Alice Huang (no relation), was passing secrets to the Chinese government in addition to encouraging the CEO to lobby for Chinese access to cutting-edge AI chips. Earlier this year, Jensen Huang [persuaded](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-26/nvidia-steps-back-into-china-market-with-first-h200-chip-sales) President Trump to allow Nvidia to resume selling the chips to China, in exchange for the U.S. government taking a 25-percent cut on all sales.

It may very well be the most successful honeypot operation in history, but it’s not the only attempt to seduce state secrets from a prominent official. In fact, Albert Einstein had his own romance with an alleged Soviet spy named Margarita Konenkova, who was reportedly after inside information on the Manhattan Project.

**Read more: “**[**The Catch 22 of Hacktivism**](https://nautil.us/the-catch-22-of-hacktivism-236770)**”**

While there are conflicting accounts of the specifics, Einstein met Konenkova a year before his wife Elsa passed away in 1936. She was married to the Russian sculptor Sergei Konenkov, who was crafting a bust of the renowned physicist. In the years that followed his wife’s death, Einstein struck up a relationship with her.

The affair didn’t come to light until half a century later when letters he penned from 1944 to 1946 documenting their tryst came to light. In them, Einstein appears to be deeply in love, sending a sketch of the “nest” (a cozy study) where the two enjoyed romantic liaisons. The smitten physicist even came up with a portmanteau couple name to refer to themselves: “Almar” (six decades before “Bennifer” and “Brangelina,” he was just as ahead of the curve in pop culture as he was in theoretical physics.)

Margarita Konenkova. _Credit: Wikimedia Commons_

Of course, as with all Cold War spycraft, whether or not this was a bona fide honeypot operation is somewhat hazy. The claims Konenkova was acting on behalf of Russian intelligence come from the memoirs of Soviet spymaster Pavel Sudoplatov, who wasn’t [entirely accurate](https://www.nytimes.com/1994/05/03/opinion/atomic-spies-or-atomic-lies.html) in his accounts. While she did introduce Einstein to Soviet vice consul Pavel Mikhailov, there’s no evidence she ever succeeded in extracting any Manhattan Project secrets from her lover. Einstein wasn’t directly involved in the project either.

The Soviets already had a much better source for intelligence on the U.S. effort to build an atomic bomb: physicist Klaus Fuchs, who was on the Project Manhattan payroll (spoilers for _Oppenheimer_). Fuchs had been passing along information to the Soviet government since the beginning of the project in 1942. Unbeknownst to Fuchs, his American colleagues Ted Hall and Saville Sax joined him in sharing secrets beginning in 1944.

These betrayals weren’t the result of steamy dalliances with Russian femme fatales. Instead they were motivated in part by a fear that the United States might have a monopoly on atomic weaponry. As we’re confronted with another civilization-ending technology, the remarkable thing about the Jensen Huang affair might not be that it worked, but that there haven’t been similar high-profile spies driven by the same fear—at least, that we know about. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

content:

# AI Company Employees Should Unionize

### ...

[![Image 5: Scott Alexander's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HTBd!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7b500d22-1176-42ad-afaa-5d72bc36a809_44x44.png)](https://substack.com/@astralcodexten)

[Scott Alexander](https://substack.com/@astralcodexten)

18 hours ago

230

128

26

Share

**I.**

Should safety-conscious employees at AI companies quit in protest, or stay and fight? The [latest argument](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/xikGZ8fuhdG6DApAo/against-sura)didn’t resolve the dispute, but it did get me in contact with organizers working on both sides.

Those planning to stay and fight are increasingly interested in labor organization. This doesn’t need to mean literal government-recognized Labor Unions. An existing group, [Coalition Of Concerned AI Staff](https://concernedaistaff.org/), is already [helping](https://andreadehlendorf.substack.com/p/across-industries-people-who-want) support interested employees and investigating other models to do more. But it might involve using laws, rights, and tactics associated with the National Labor Relations Act and the labor movement.

You may remember stories of bitter unionization battles at places like Starbucks, but AI workers can probably route around that. The toughest labor disputes happen in fields where the employer could easily fire all the organized workers and replace them from a bottomless pool of faceless scabs: although this is illegal, everyone needs to be maximally lawyered-up to prevent it. But there are so few skilled AI researchers that these laws are hardly necessary; if a dozen top AI researchers threaten to walk, it doesn’t matter whether Section P Sub-Section Q forces the AI company to negotiate - the AI company will want to negotiate. This cuts through the red tape that intimidates workers in less blessed fields[1](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-1); AI researchers could likely get away with only the package of rights provided by informal “concerted activity”, defined as two or more workers doing anything vaguely labor-activism-shaped. Just put up a sign somewhere saying “OpenAI Safety Union” and get at least two employees to stand behind it, and it counts.

(even the word “union” is unnecessary; if employees felt like it was too adversarial, they could call it “OpenAI Research Council” or something)

Once an organization existed, the law would ban the company from firing people simply for being part of it, or talking to other members, or planning demands or actions together. It also couldn’t fire workers for striking over workplace conditions[2](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-2).

Does the “workplace conditions” requirement rule out most forms of safety activism? Not necessarily: many safety issues double as workplace issues, including whistleblower protections, auditing requirements, and safety team staffing. Most of all, fears of recursive self-improvement are naturally workplace-related: whatever else RSI does to the world, it will also automate AI researcher positions. This would be a popular starting issue that might attract even non-alignment-pilled colleagues.

But even if some safety issue has no workplace relevance at all, employees can still strike over it; they only lose their protection against being fired. And good AI researchers are worth tens of millions of dollars each and nearly irreplaceable, so AI companies are already averse to firing dozens of them at once. And any attempt to fire striking AI researchers would likely make national news and be a PR disaster. So the legal protection against being fired isn’t doing most of the work anyway, and AI employee organizations could strike over issues without direct workplace relevance if they wanted[3](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-3).

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bdM9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F216275dc-2bdd-484c-9959-9fe3d3538c48_941x550.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bdM9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F216275dc-2bdd-484c-9959-9fe3d3538c48_941x550.png)

What if employees think their company already does a good job prioritizing safety? Then they should organize in order to give their already-virtuous company more options. Negotiations between unions get less antitrust scrutiny than negotiations between companies, so workers can forge deals to slow research or prioritize safety even when executives’ hands are tied.

For example, suppose that OpenAI leadership orders its researchers to switch to a less-monitorable looped transformer design. A safety-conscious employee union might ask further questions, or mutually refuse to pursue this. If Sam Altman said that they _had_ to build a looped transformer, or else Anthropic would build it first and beat them, the organizers could call up their friends at the Anthropic Employee Union and ask whether they would go on strike if Anthropic built a looped transformer. If the Anthropic Employee Union said yes, then the two unions could present a united front, and their companies wouldn’t have to worry about the other company racing ahead.[4](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-4)[5](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-5)

Although on its own this has limited value - Meta or DeepSeek could still build the looped transformer - these union deals could also provide a standard that the industry could rally around, or a clear starting point for government intervention. In an extreme case, two unions could negotiate the beginnings of a pause deal, force it on their parent companies, and the government could take note and make it part of a future international deal.

What else could unions or union-like organizations work toward?

*   Upholding normal protections around discipline and firing. In October, OpenAI [fired](https://x.com/ZeffMax/status/2113438537798525372)three safety researchers after accusing them of leaking information on the company’s experiments with [potentially-dangerous looped transformers](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-specter-of-neuralese); these accusations [now seem to be false](https://x.com/RyanGreenblatt/status/2113649836100931761), with the most likely scenario being that OpenAI was angry about the leak and fired some people in the vicinity of the problem to make a point. If OpenAI employees had a union, the company might have to be more careful about firing employees under false pretenses.

*   Holding companies to the commitments they made during September’s excitement around [Pacing The Frontier](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier), for example, demanding that they hire independent evaluators with employee-level access by such-and-such a time.

*   Demanding transparency, eg about compute allocation [as described here](https://blog.aifutures.org/p/verified-compute-allocation-disclosures), or about [the information necessary to](https://x.com/METR_Evals/status/2118412194702598339) measure the speed of recursive self-improvement.

*   Acting as an independent voice holding companies to their commitments. This is another one that works even if (especially if?) employees already trust their company leadership. Currently, companies struggle to make credible promises because there’s nobody inside who can enforce them. A union that threatened to investigate or raise a fuss if a promise were broken could help executives be taken seriously.

**II.**

For people taking the other route - whistleblowing or quitting - my contacts recommend talking to [Psst](https://psst.org/), a nonprofit that provides legal advice for concerned tech workers.

Whistleblowing is a fraught process. Your company has more experience catching and neutralizing whistleblowers than you have being one, and if you’re working on your own, then you will probably fail to cover your tracks (did you know companies look to see how many times different employees checked leaked documents, on the grounds that someone who’s agonizing about whether to whistleblow about them probably reads them more often than most?) Another classic mistake is to complain about something internally, then whistleblow after your complaints are not taken seriously; it’s not hard for companies to connect the dots and realize that the complainer and the whistleblower are probably the same person. Psst has more experience with this than you or your company, and can walk you through the process.

Even if you’re thinking of quitting, Psst may be able to help. You may have more options than you thought, like threatening to quit unless you get the thing you want. And if you do decide to quit, you may want to do it in the most effective way possible - make a splash on your way out, like [Jacob Coxon](https://time.com/article/2026/09/15/ai-anthropic-researcher-quits-coxon-slowdown/) did. This requires some basic media literacy, and Psst will connect you with the people who can give it to you.

Contact Psst by messaging **@PsstLegal.01** on Signal on a personal device without any employer spyware. The person on the other end will be a lawyer, and your conversation with them will be confidential.

Whatever AI employees do, they should do it soon. RSI could start making them obsolete [as soon as next year](https://www.aifuturesmodel.com/), so they may never have this amount of leverage again.

[1](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-anchor-1)

To become an official majority union, a union must win the support of a majority of workers in a secret ballot. This gives them a few extra rights like forcing companies to bargain with them (the companies don’t have to agree to any bargain, but can get in trouble for bargaining in bad faith if they’re pointlessly recalcitrant), but also restricts the union’s ability to legally advocate for non-workplace-related causes. A union can also get some of these rights by having an employer voluntarily recognize them. We don’t expect that AI company unions will go down either of these paths.

[2](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-anchor-2)

Companies do have the option of replacing striking workers during a strike, then firing them after the strike because their jobs are already filled. But frontier AI researchers are hard to replace en masse, so they may not need to worry about this.

[3](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-anchor-3)

If AI destroyed the world, wouldn’t that negatively impact working conditions at AI companies? Legal theory only considers a generally destructive event detrimental to working conditions if it would damage the conditions more than it damaged everything else, so this argument probably wouldn’t hold.

[4](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-anchor-4)

This particular example may straddle the border of legality; the situation might change depending on how much it seemed like a nod-and-wink deal between Sam and Dario, and whether it was a purely political demand (as in this case) vs. had a plausible connection to working conditions. I would still be excited about borderline-legal examples, because court cases might last longer than my timeline to AGI anyway, the publicity would be pure positive, and any sanctions if it turned out illegal would likely be weak.

[5](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ai-company-employees-should-unionize#footnote-anchor-5)

Legally recognized unions get more antitrust exemptions and bargaining rights, and potentially could bring both Anthropic and OpenAI to the table and hammer something out, but they are under closer scrutiny to ensure that they focus on workplace conditions rather than issues of general interest.
